Sweeps

A sweep runs the sheet once for each value of an input and collects results from every run. Help › Examples › Sweeps opens the Rankine cycle of A complete cycle in the Sweep view and runs the sweep below.

Sweeping one input

% The sweep runs the sheet once for each value of T_1, an input of the sheet.
sweep T_1 = 400:20:600 [C]
% record keeps these variables from every run, for the results table.
record eta, x_2, w_net, bwr
% plot draws one figure per line.
plot eta vs T_1
plot x_2 vs T_1
% Move the slider to step through the runs; every pane follows it.

Dome runs the sheet eleven times, for T_1 = 400, 420, … 600 °C. On the first chart, eta rises from 0.32214 at 400 °C to 0.3478 at 600 °C.

  1. Write the sweep in the editor of the Sweep view. The sheet stays as it is written.
  2. sweep T_1 = 400:20:600 [C] gives the values as start:step:stop. A list works too: sweep p_b = 40, 70, 100 [bar].
  3. Write the unit after the values, a unit of the same kind as the input's. The values need a unit whenever the input has one on the sheet.
  4. An input written as a plain number, such as eta_t = 0.86, takes plain values: sweep eta_t = 0.80:0.05:0.90 runs as written.
  5. The swept name must be an input of the sheet: a line name = number [unit], or a number in a state line. The x = 0 of state 3 is one.
  6. record names the variables kept from each run, for the results table. A plotted variable is kept without being named.
  7. Each plot y vs x line draws a chart, with a tab of its own above the charts. Without a plot line, the chart shows the first two recorded variables.
  8. plot eta, x_2 vs T_1 draws two variables on one chart, with an axis for each, left and right.
  9. Run, in the header, runs the sweep again after an edit, as does ⌘Enter (CtrlEnter on Windows and Linux).

Reading the results

sweep p_b = 40:10:120 [bar]
record eta, x_2, w_net, bwr
plot eta vs p_b
plot x_2 vs p_b

The example ends by suggesting this sweep of the boiler pressure. Dome runs nine values: eta rises from 0.31875 at 40 bar to 0.35285 at 120 bar, and x_2 falls from 0.93867 to 0.8656.

  1. The slider under the chart steps through the runs, and a dashed line on the chart marks the run it is on. Beside the slider, Dome lists the recorded values of that run.
  2. Every pane follows the slider: the sheet's values, the Workspace, the states table and the figures show the run it is on.
  3. A click on the chart moves the slider to the nearest run. A click on a row of the results table moves it to that run.
  4. The results table has a row for each run. Copy, above the table, copies it as tab-separated text.
  5. Any pane of the Sweep view can show a figure of the sheet: choose it in the pane's menu.
  6. Leaving the Sweep view returns every pane to the sheet as written.

The shot shows the example's own sweep, with the slider at its last run, T_1 = 600 °C, and the T–s diagram of that run.

Families of curves

sweep T_1 = 400:20:600 [C]
sweep p_b = 40, 70, 100 [bar]
record eta, x_2
plot eta vs T_1
plot x_2 vs T_1

With a second sweep line, Dome runs every combination of the two, here 33 runs. Each chart has a curve for each p_b: at 600 °C, eta is 0.3299, 0.3478 and 0.35845 for 40, 70 and 100 bar.

  1. A plot is drawn against one of the swept variables, with a curve for each value of the other. The legend here reads p_b = 40 bar, p_b = 70 bar and p_b = 100 bar.
  2. plot eta vs p_b draws a curve for each value of T_1 instead.
  3. Each value of p_b has its own color and marker shape, the same in every chart. With one variable plotted, it also has its own line style. With several, the line style tells the variables apart.
  4. Up to five curves stay apart in a grayscale print.
  5. There is a slider for each swept variable. Moving one keeps the other at its value, so the run moves along one curve. The markers of that run are filled.
  6. The results table lists p_b, then T_1. Its rows are grouped by p_b, the variable that makes the curves of the first plot.
  7. A sweep has two sweep lines at most, and 2000 runs at most.

A run that fails

sweep p_c = 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1 [bar]
record eta, x_2
plot eta vs p_c

The first run, at 0.005 bar, fails. The other runs give eta = 0.38432, 0.35275 and 0.33711. Under the sweep editor, Dome lists the failed run:

p_c = 0.005 bar: state 2s: water: no state has these values of p and s within the property data (0.01 °C to 1926.85 °C, up to 10000 bar)

0.005 bar is below the pressure of water's triple point, 0.006117 bar. Below that pressure, water is never liquid. An isentropic expansion from state 1 to 0.005 bar would end as a mix of ice and vapor. Dome's water has no ice: its data start at 0.01 °C.

  1. A run that fails has no values. It leaves a gap in each curve, and its row of the results table shows a red – for each value.
  2. The list under the sweep editor gives each failed run's inputs and first error. A click on the inputs moves the slider to that run.
  3. The list shows six failed runs at most, then the number of the others.
  4. Below the editor, Dome counts the runs, the time they took and the runs that failed.

Exporting a sweep

sweep T_1 = 400:100:600 [C]
sweep p_b = 40, 70, 100 [bar]
record eta
plot eta vs T_1

Export, the button above the chart, writes this sweep as a MATLAB script among other formats. The script holds eta as a matrix, with a row for each T_1 and a column for each p_b:

T_1 = [400 500 600];  % °C
p_b = [40 70 100];  % bar
% eta(i, j) is the run with T_1(i) and p_b(j).
eta = [0.303495 0.322144 0.332342
       0.316065 0.33451 0.345201
       0.329898 0.3478 0.35845];
  1. Export writes the chart as PNG, SVG or PDF, or copies it as an image.
  2. It also copies the data as tab-separated text, or writes it as CSV or a MATLAB script. The data has one row per run, as in the results table.
  3. The MATLAB script draws each plot, with one plot call per curve. With two sweep lines, the rows of each matrix follow the variable of the first plot.
  4. A published report can include a sweep that has run: see Publishing.

When Dome refuses

A message about a sweep line appears under the sweep editor, with the line's number. Each entry gives a sweep line, the message and what to change.

A swept name that is not an input

sweep w_net = 1000:100:1200 [kJ/kg]

w_net is not an input of the sheet (a line w_net = number [unit], or a number in a state line)

The sheet finds w_net from other values, so a sweep cannot set it. Sweep an input that w_net depends on, such as T_1 or p_b.

Too many runs

sweep T_1 = 400:0.05:600 [C]

4001 runs is too many; use a larger step (at most 2000 runs)

Use a larger step. With two sweep lines, the message gives the product, such as 51 × 81 = 4131 runs, and asks for fewer values.

Values without a unit

sweep T_1 = 400:100:600

the values of T_1 need a unit, as T_1 = 520 [C] on the sheet has one: sweep T_1 = 400:100:600 [C]

Add the unit the message gives. Before Dome 0.1.17 these values ran as 400 K, 500 K and 600 K, with no message.

A unit of another kind

sweep T_1 = 400:100:600 [bar]

[bar] is not a unit of T_1, which the sheet gives in [C]

Write a unit of temperature, such as [C] or [K].

A range that runs the wrong way

sweep T_1 = 600:20:400 [C]

write a range as start:step:stop, e.g. 320:20:600

A step of 20 cannot go from 600 down to 400. Write 400:20:600, or 600:-20:400 for the same values in the other order.

A plot against a third variable

sweep T_1 = 400:100:600 [C]
sweep p_b = 40, 70 [bar]
plot eta vs w_net

with two sweep lines, a plot is drawn against one of them: plot eta vs T_1 or plot eta vs p_b

Plot against T_1 or p_b. With one sweep line, a plot against a recorded variable such as w_net is allowed.

A recorded name the sheet does not have

record eta, effic

not in the sheet: effic

The runs go ahead, and the column of effic shows – in every row. Correct the name to one the sheet defines.

A misspelled sweep line

sweeps T_1 = 400:20:600 [C]

a sweep has lines "sweep name = start:step:stop [unit]", "record a, b" and "plot a, b vs name"

Dome reads only these three kinds of line, and comments. Correct the first word to sweep.
